span.label: Groups trained on a spectral versus a spatial cue showed a double dissociation in brain activity, ventral areas for the spectral group and dorsal areas for the spatial group, despite identical stimuli.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Behavioural benefit after training was specific to the trained acoustic feature rather than general.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The group difference in cortical source activity appeared within roughly 100 ms of sound onset, which the authors read as a pre-stimulus attentional bias toward the trained feature.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Because both groups faced identical stimulus-response demands, the difference cannot be explained as procedural learning.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: After training the two cues no longer combined additively: the trained cue alone captured almost all of the benefit available from both cues together.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The two groups improved equally with practice overall, so the feature-specific effect is not an artefact of one group simply learning more.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The authors claim priority for showing feature-specific plasticity in human brain activity after under an hour of training.
